intro: A G-major minuet steps aside for a musette, a dance over a bagpipe-like drone. When the minuet comes back, Ravel lets the two dances share the keyboard.

sections.label: A · The G-major minuet
sections.mNote: An ornamented melody above a gently moving bass

sections.label: B · Musette over a drone
sections.mNote: G minor, with held bass notes and moving chords

sections.label: A′ · Two dances together
sections.mNote: The minuet returns above the musette’s chords

sections.label: Coda · Arpeggios beneath the melody
sections.mNote: The left hand flows, then the dance slows to stillness

cues.title: The minuet’s little ornament
cues.text: A tiny turn decorates the melody’s first note. The tune moves lightly through three beats while the bass follows its own path underneath. Ravel marks the G-major opening pianissimo and Allegro moderato.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Menuet, p. 20; Piano Practical Editions, bars 1–8, p. 34. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/48/IMSLP560971-PMLP4975-Le_Tombeau_de_Couperin.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Jean Dreyfus’s family home
cues.text: The Menuet remembers Jean Dreyfus, killed in the First World War. His stepmother, Madame Fernand Dreyfus, receives Ravel’s letters from the front and later takes him into the family home in Normandy. There he recovers from military service and works on this suite.
cues.evidence: The dedication is recorded by the BnF: https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb13917720k. Family relationship, wartime correspondence and Normandy stay: Eric T. Williams, Kansas City Symphony programme, 5–7 April 2024, pp. 5–6. https://www.kcsymphony.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/FY24-CS10-Program-Book-Digital-2024-04-05.pdf

cues.title: A bagpipe beneath the chords
cues.text: The central dance is a Musette. Its G-minor chords move over a drone, the keyboard’s imitation of a bagpipe. The B♭ darkens the tune, while E♮ gives the minor scale an unexpectedly bright sixth step.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Menuet, Musette; Piano Practical Editions, bars 33–48, p. 35. The edition’s commentary identifies G Dorian, a minor mode with a raised sixth.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The dances meet
cues.text: The minuet’s first melody returns in G major. Beneath it, the left hand keeps the musette’s chords. The piano now plays both dances at once: the ornamented tune above, the quieter chordal steps below.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Menuet, p. 22; Piano Practical Editions, bars 73–80, p. 36, superimposes the minuet melody and musette accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Arpeggios open the hands
cues.text: The left hand turns from chords to flowing arpeggios. The melody stretches above them as the hands spread farther apart. Ravel builds one last broad phrase before drawing the piano back to pianissimo.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Menuet, p. 23; Piano Practical Editions, bars 105–120, p. 38: arpeggiated bass, crescendo and the return to pp.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Keys pressed without sound
cues.text: The closing page asks for much slowing, then Très lent. At the end, Ravel tells the pianist to press keys silently. The pedal clears, leaving only the notes whose dampers remain raised to ring into the final G-major chord.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Menuet, final bars; Piano Practical Editions, bars 124–128, p. 38, and commentary on bar 127: sans faire vibrer means to depress the keys silently.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: G major turns towards the bagpipe
transitions.how: The minuet’s repeated strain closes, and the piano begins the Musette softly. G remains the home note, but B♭ replaces B♮. Held bass notes support the moving chords; E♮ keeps the new G-minor dance in the Dorian mode. The three-beat bar continues.
transitions.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), pp. 20–21; Piano Practical Editions, Menuet, bars 31–40, p. 35.

transitions.title: The minuet returns above the musette
transitions.how: The musette subsides to pianissimo. The piano restores G major and raises the opening melody above the musette’s chordal accompaniment. Its grace notes and long slurs belong to the minuet; the left hand continues the middle dance’s steps.
transitions.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Menuet, p. 22; Piano Practical Editions, bars 65–80, p. 36.

transitions.title: The bass starts to flow
transitions.how: Ravel keeps the upper melody and replaces the left-hand chords with arpeggios. A gradual crescendo carries the hands farther across the keyboard, then the line falls back to pianissimo. The final G-major close follows after increasingly slow phrases.
transitions.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Menuet, p. 23; Piano Practical Editions, bars 105–128, p. 38.

composer.epithet: He made a ballet from two tunes and a snare drum, and gave his war dead a suite of dances.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery. His mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He kept returning to the Basque coast, and Spain kept returning in his music: the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera that rocks through the Rapsodie espagnole, the clocks ticking in a Toledo shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. Two teachers then understood him: André Gedalge, who gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and Fauré, whose composition class he entered in January 1898. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, became the pianist his music needed. Viñes gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces their composer could never have played with comparable command.
